newsitem.title: INDIA: Asian rivals slow down India textile export growth.
newsitem.headline: Asian rivals slow down India textile export growth.

text.p: India is facing stiff competition from its Asian neighbours in the textile trade, its biggest export earner, and exports are already showing signs of losing momentum, a leading industry body said on Wednesday.

The Indian Cotton Mills Federation (ICMF) said figures for the 1995/96 year, running April to March, showed that annual growth in textile exports had taken a downward turn after robust rises in the early 1990s.
"In the three-year period 1992/93 to 1994/95, there was average annual growth of 20 percent in textile exports in terms of U.S. dollars," said D. Lakshminarayanaswamy, chairman of the federation.

The growth in overall textile exports fell sharply to five percent in 1995/96, Lakshminarayanaswamy told the ICMF's annual general meeting, with India's exports of garments actually falling for the first time in recent years.
"This certainly is not a happy situation in a year of record production of yarn and fabrics," he said, citing tough competition from elsewhere in Asia.
The ICMF represents textile trade and industry associations across India.

India exported textiles valued at around 300 billion rupees ($8.4 billion) in 1995/96. Textiles continued to be the single largest contributor to India's foreign exchange earnings, accounting for more than 27 percent of Indian commodity exports.
Exports of spun yarn, at $1.22 billion in 1995/96, were 26 percent higher than in the year-ago period, the ICMF chief said.
"This is the only item which has displayed buoyancy during the year," he said.
India's exports of clothes fell, though marginally, to $4.52 billion in 1995/96 from $4.54 billion a year ago, Lakshminarayanaswamy said.
"All these years, clothing exports have been our mainstay and therefore all concerned should put their heads together to study and analyse factors responsible for the slowdown," he said.
The ICMF chairman said India was facing stiff competition from China, Pakistan, Indonesia, Thailand and Malaysia and even new entrants like Vietnam.
Indian industry badly needed modernisation and an end to archaic government controls, he said.
He said any strategy would have to address issues such as upgrading technology, improving quality, cutting costs and conducting aggressive marketing, the chairman said.
He decried quantitative restrictions on cotton yarn exports by the government "on the specious plea of protecting the interests of handlooms (manually operated spinning units)".

"It is ironical that, while on the one hand India has been advocating in various international fora for a total removal of the quota regime, on the other hand there is a self-imposed internal ceiling for export of cotton yarns."
India's concessional tax rates for small units also hurt its international competitiveness, Lakshminarayanaswamy said.
